draft.title: Responses to international crime
card: International Criminal Court
The ICC is a permanent court in The Hague. It tries individuals accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Limits
The ICC can act only where a state has joined it or the UN Security Council has referred a situation. It is meant to step in when national courts cannot or will not act.
Extradition
One country formally hands a suspect or convicted person to another country, so that person can face trial or serve a sentence there. It usually relies on a treaty.
Police cooperation
Police forces share information and work together across borders. Agencies such as the Australian Federal Police and Interpol help with transnational crimes like drug trafficking and cybercrime.
draft.remember: The ICC tries the gravest crimes against international law. Extradition and police cooperation tackle crime that crosses borders.

a.q: A suspect accused of drug trafficking is arrested in Thailand. Australia asks Thailand to send the suspect to Australia for trial. What is this process called?
a.why: Extradition is the formal handing over of a suspect from one country to another for trial. Police cooperation is a tempting answer, but it covers sharing information and working together, not formally transferring a suspect.
a.clue: Think of a formal request to hand over a person.

b.q: A military leader is accused of ordering the killing of a whole ethnic group. Which response fits this crime best?
opts: A trial of the leader before the ICC
Extradition of the leader to face a drug trafficking charge
Interpol sharing data to trace a cybercrime network
A national court always hearing the case first and only
b.why: Genocide is one of the crimes the ICC tries, and it tries individuals. Extradition and police cooperation are tools for transnational crime such as drug trafficking and cybercrime, which this case is not.
b.clue: Match the type of crime to the body that tries it.

b.best: A trial of the leader before the ICC

problems.detail: The claim that the ICC 'can act only where a state has joined it or the UN Security Council has referred a situation' is oversimplified. Jurisdiction depends on the territorial state or the accused's state being a party. A non-member state can also accept jurisdiction by declaration (Article 12(3), as Ukraine did before joining). The 'only' makes the statement inaccurate.
The card lists genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity as the crimes the ICC tries. Since 2018 the ICC can also try the crime of aggression, so the list is incomplete for current study.

The option 'A national court always hearing the case first and only' is ungrammatical and confusing. Its 'always' and 'only' flag it as wrong without the student needing the idea. It also half-echoes the card's complementarity point, that national courts act first, so it could confuse a careful student.

check.summary: Both questions have clear, correct answers: Extradition and an ICC trial. The card oversimplifies ICC jurisdiction with 'only' and leaves out the crime of aggression, and option b's 'always ... first and only' is awkwardly worded and gives itself away as wrong.

proposal.title: Responses to international crime
card: International Criminal Court
The ICC is a permanent court in The Hague. It tries individuals accused of genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and, since 2018, the crime of aggression.
Jurisdiction

The ICC usually acts when a crime happens in a member state or the accused is from one. A non-member state can accept its jurisdiction, and the UN Security Council can refer a situation to it. It is a court of last resort, stepping in when national courts are unable or unwilling to act.
Extradition
One country formally hands a suspect or convicted person to another country, so that person can face trial or serve a sentence there. It usually relies on a treaty.
Police cooperation
Police forces share information and work together across borders. Agencies such as the Australian Federal Police and Interpol help with transnational crimes like drug trafficking and cybercrime.
proposal.remember: The ICC tries the gravest crimes against international law. Extradition and police cooperation tackle crime that crosses borders.

a.q: A suspect accused of drug trafficking is arrested in Thailand. Australia asks Thailand to send the suspect to Australia for trial. What is this process called?
opts: Extradition of the suspect for trial
Referral of the case to the ICC
A trial of the suspect in The Hague
a.why: Extradition is the formal handing over of a suspect from one country to another for trial. Police cooperation is tempting, but it covers sharing information and working together, not formally transferring a person.
a.clue: Think of a formal request to hand over a person.

b.q: A military leader is accused of ordering the killing of a whole ethnic group. Which of these is set up to try the leader for this crime?
b.why: This is genocide, which the ICC tries, and it tries individuals. The UN Security Council is tempting, but it can only refer a situation to the ICC, not try anyone. Interpol and the AFP are police bodies, not courts.
b.clue: Which of these is a court?
